options.text: Indefinite cabergoline at the highest tolerated dose, because after menopause the risk of tumour growth rises markedly
options.why: The consensus says that after menopause a microprolactinoma may need no intervention; menopause increases the chance of resolution (weak).

options.text: Scheduled transsphenoidal surgery, because after menopause the risk of hypopituitarism that limits it in young women no longer applies
options.why: The consensus does not propose routine surgery in this setting or claim that this risk disappears.

options.text: Gadolinium MRI every 6 months for life, because prolactin stops being a reliable marker after menopause
options.why: The consensus proposes follow-up with annual prolactin, not 6-monthly MRI.

options.text: It may need no intervention and can be followed with annual prolactin (weak)
options.why: Correct: this is the consensus proposal.

items.explanation: After menopause, the 2023 Pituitary Society considers that a microprolactinoma may need no intervention and can be followed with annual prolactin (weak); menopause also increases the chance of resolution after agonist withdrawal (weak).

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman (fictional case) has been on cabergoline 0.5 mg weekly for 4 months; her partner reports she has started gambling online and buying impulsively. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society recommend?

options.text: Stop the drug or adjust the dose, because this is a recognised neuropsychiatric effect of agonists (strong)
options.why: Correct: this is the management the consensus recommends.

options.text: Keep the dose unchanged, because at only 0.5 mg weekly an impulse control disorder cannot be due to cabergoline
options.why: Impulsivity is not dose-related, so a low dose does not exclude it.

options.text: Dismiss it as a cause, because impulse control disorders with agonists have only been described in men
options.why: They are more frequent in men but occur in both sexes.

options.text: Add an antipsychotic such as risperidone to control the behaviour and keep cabergoline at the same dose
options.why: Risperidone raises prolactin, and the consensus asks for the agonist to be stopped or adjusted.

items.explanation: Agonists can cause compulsive buying, gambling, aggression, mood changes or hypersexuality; if they appear, the drug should be stopped or the dose adjusted (strong). They are more frequent in men but occur in both sexes, are not dose-related, and the partner and family should also be asked.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) starting cabergoline is worried about nausea. Which measures does the 2023 Pituitary Society suggest to improve tolerability?

options.text: Take it fasting in the morning at the full dose from day one, so that the effect is faster and the nausea lasts less
options.why: The consensus suggests the opposite: at bedtime or with food and starting low (weak).

options.text: Switch straight to bromocriptine, which according to the consensus statements causes less nausea than cabergoline in the comparative trial
options.why: In the trial cited by the Chinese consensus, bromocriptine caused more nausea (≈ 50% versus 31%).

options.text: Warn before starting about the frequent mild adverse effects (strong) and take it at bedtime or with food, starting low (weak)
options.why: Correct: it combines the recommendation to inform with the tolerability suggestions.

options.text: Add an antiemetic such as metoclopramide routinely during the first weeks of treatment
options.why: Metoclopramide raises prolactin, and the consensus does not propose routine antiemetics.

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society asks clinicians to warn before starting about the frequent mild adverse effects (gastrointestinal, dizziness, fatigue) (strong) and suggests taking it at bedtime or with food and starting low (weak). If intolerance persists, it suggests another D2 agonist such as quinagolide (weak); in Spain, quinagolide is no longer authorised (revoked in February 2024). The Dostinex product information also advises taking it with food.

items.stem: According to the 2025 Chinese consensus, in whom should impulse control disorders with agonists be explained and monitored especially?

options.text: In postmenopausal women over 60, because the risk depends on age and cumulative agonist dose
options.why: The consensus highlights people under 40, and the Pituitary Society notes it is not dose-related.

options.text: In men, people under 40, and those with a history of smoking, alcohol, anxiety or depression
options.why: Correct: these are the groups the consensus names; it cites a highly variable incidence (9.8–52%).

options.text: Only in those taking more than 2 mg of cabergoline weekly, the threshold above which these disorders appear
options.why: There is no dose threshold: the Pituitary Society notes impulsivity is not dose-related. 2 mg weekly is the echocardiography threshold.

options.text: Only in patients with schizophrenia on antipsychotics, because outside that group the incidence is below 1%
options.why: The consensus cites an incidence of 9.8–52% without limiting it to that group; the 1% figure is wrong.

items.explanation: The 2025 Chinese consensus cites a highly variable incidence of impulse control disorders (9.8–52%) and asks for information and monitoring especially in men, people under 40, and those with a history of smoking, alcohol, anxiety or depression.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman (fictional case) with macroprolactinoma will need long-term cabergoline 3 mg weekly. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society propose regarding echocardiography?

options.text: Echocardiography only after 5–6 years of treatment, as with low doses, because valve risk does not depend on dose
options.why: That schedule is for doses ≤ 2.0 mg weekly; with higher doses the consensus proposes a baseline echocardiogram.

options.text: No echocardiography, because valvulopathy has only been described with the doses used in Parkinson’s disease
options.why: With long-term doses > 2.0 mg weekly, the consensus proposes baseline and repeat echocardiography.

options.text: Annual cardiac auscultation without echocardiography, which most of the panel considers sufficient at any dose
options.why: Most of the panel considered annual cardiac examination unnecessary; it does not propose it as a substitute.

options.text: Baseline echocardiography, repeated every 2–3 years while she stays on those doses (weak)
options.why: Correct: this is the proposal for long-term doses > 2.0 mg weekly.

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society proposes baseline echocardiography if long-term cabergoline > 2.0 mg weekly is anticipated, repeated every 2–3 years at those doses; with ≤ 2.0 mg weekly, after 5–6 years; and with a murmur, echocardiography (all weak).

items.stem: Which statement reflects what the 2025 Chinese consensus says about valve monitoring?

options.text: It indicates echocardiography with doses > 2 mg/week, more than 5 years of treatment, age > 50 or a murmur, and does not support routine echocardiographic monitoring with bromocriptine
options.why: Correct: these are the criteria given in its text.

options.text: It recommends annual echocardiography for every patient on any agonist, including bromocriptine, because of a valvulopathy incidence above 10%
options.why: It cites an incidence of 0.11% in prolactinoma and does not support routine monitoring with bromocriptine; the 10% figure is wrong.

options.text: It advises against baseline echocardiography because cabergoline-associated valvulopathy has not been described in prolactinoma patients
options.why: Its text advises a baseline echocardiogram and cites an incidence of 0.11% in prolactinoma.

options.text: It sets the dose threshold at 1 mg weekly and proposes repeating echocardiography every 6 months above it
options.why: The threshold is 2 mg weekly and repetition every 2–3 years.

items.explanation: The 2025 Chinese consensus cites a cabergoline-associated valvulopathy incidence of 0.11% in prolactinoma, advises a baseline echocardiogram in its text, indicates echocardiography with doses > 2 mg/week, more than 5 years of treatment, age > 50 or a murmur, proposes repeating it every 2–3 years and does not support routine monitoring with bromocriptine. Its graded recommendation is low certainty; weak.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) stops cabergoline after meeting withdrawal criteria. How does the 2023 Pituitary Society propose to follow her up?

options.text: A single prolactin at 6 months and final discharge if normal, because relapses after that time are exceptional
options.why: Follow-up is lifelong: every 3 months in the first year and then annually.

options.text: Prolactin every 3 months in the first year and then annually (or sooner if symptoms recur), lifelong; if it relapses, the agonist usually works again
options.why: Correct: this is the consensus schedule (strong for the agonist working again after relapse).

options.text: MRI every 3 months during the first year, because prolactin does not detect relapse until the tumour has regrown
options.why: The consensus proposes monitoring with prolactin, not quarterly MRI.

options.text: No monitoring unless symptoms, and if it relapses, surgery straight away, because after relapse the agonist is no longer effective
options.why: After relapse the agonist usually works again (strong).

items.explanation: After withdrawal, the 2023 Pituitary Society proposes prolactin every 3 months in the first year and then annually (or sooner if symptoms recur), lifelong; if it relapses, the agonist usually works again (strong), and menopause or a pregnancy increases the chance of resolution (weak).

items.stem: Which pairing of remission figures after agonist withdrawal is correct?

options.text: Pituitary Society: about 80% of patients stay in remission after stopping cabergoline, so withdrawal should be tried in everyone at 6 months
options.why: It is the reverse: about one in five (≈ 20%) stays in remission.

options.text: Chinese consensus: 55% in micro- and 43% in macroadenomas in all patients who stop, regardless of dose or treatment duration
options.why: The 55% and 43% are Pituitary Society figures, and only for the most favourable subgroup.

options.text: Chinese consensus (meta-analysis): 21% in micro- and 16% in macroadenomas, 34% if treatment lasted more than 2 years, and 35% with cabergoline versus 20% with bromocriptine
options.why: Correct: these are the figures from the meta-analysis it cites.

options.text: Pituitary Society: remission is higher with high maintenance doses and less than 1 year of treatment, because the tumour then does not develop resistance
options.why: The predictors are a low maintenance dose, more than 2 years of treatment and substantial adenoma shrinkage (strong).

items.explanation: 2023 Pituitary Society: about one in five stays in remission; in the most favourable subgroup (small non-invasive adenoma, normal prolactin and tumour shrinkage after at least 2 years of cabergoline 0.25–0.50 mg weekly), about 55% of micro- and 43% of macroprolactinomas. The Chinese consensus cites a meta-analysis: 21% in micro-, 16% in macroadenomas, 34% with more than 2 years and 35% with cabergoline versus 20% with bromocriptine.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman (fictional case) on haloperidol has a prolactin 15 times the upper limit. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society indicate?

options.text: Attribute it to the antipsychotic without further work-up, because first-generation antipsychotics raise prolactin above 20 times the limit
options.why: Exceeding 10 times the limit is uncommon with antipsychotics; the 20-times figure is wrong.

options.text: Stop haloperidol abruptly without consulting psychiatry and repeat prolactin in a week
options.why: The consensus asks for collaboration with psychiatry (strong).

options.text: Prescribe high-dose cabergoline to normalise prolactin, with no imaging because the drug cause is obvious
options.why: Above 10 times the limit, prolactinoma should be suspected and MRI is indicated.

options.text: Suspect a prolactinoma, because more than 10 times the limit is uncommon with antipsychotics, and order MRI
options.why: Correct: this is the threshold the consensus sets (strong).

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society recommends suspecting a prolactinoma if prolactin exceeds 10 times the upper limit, because this is uncommon in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia (strong). MRI is indicated with prolactin > 10 times the limit, mass symptoms or non-gonadal pituitary deficits. Management requires collaboration with psychiatry (strong).

items.stem: What does the 2023 Pituitary Society recommend before starting an antipsychotic, and how often does hyperprolactinaemia occur with these drugs?

options.text: Nothing in particular before starting; hyperprolactinaemia occurs in under 5% and takes more than a year to develop
options.why: It occurs in 30–75% within the first 3 months; the 5% figure is wrong.

options.text: Measure prolactin before starting it (strong); hyperprolactinaemia occurs in 30–75% within the first 3 months and resolves within 48–96 hours of withdrawal
options.why: Correct: these are the consensus data.

options.text: Order a baseline pituitary MRI in everyone, because 30–75% develop a drug-induced microadenoma in the first months
options.why: The 30–75% refers to hyperprolactinaemia, not adenomas; the consensus does not propose routine baseline MRI.

options.text: Start preventive cabergoline together with the antipsychotic, since this prevents hyperprolactinaemia in most cases
options.why: The consensus does not propose preventive agonists; their use in these patients needs caution and psychiatric input (weak).

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society recommends measuring prolactin before starting an antipsychotic (strong). Hyperprolactinaemia occurs in 30–75% within the first 3 months and resolves within 48–96 hours of withdrawal.

items.stem: A 30-year-old woman (fictional case) with macroprolactinoma wants to become pregnant. What do the consensus statements recommend before conception?

options.text: Try to conceive immediately without prior treatment, because pregnancy itself shrinks macroadenomas
options.why: It is the reverse: prior treatment lowers the risk of growth in pregnancy (from 18% to 4.7%, according to the Chinese consensus).

options.text: Mandatory surgery for every macroprolactinoma before conception, without first trying the agonist, to avoid any growth
options.why: Surgery is considered if there is no agonist response, and the risk of hypopituitarism must be explained.

options.text: Confirm agonist response before conception and consider surgery if there is none (Pituitary Society, strong); the Chinese consensus suggests shrinking it to microadenoma size
options.why: Correct: both ask for the tumour to be shrunk before pregnancy.

options.text: Switch from cabergoline to bromocriptine, because both consensus statements consider cabergoline contraindicated when trying to conceive
options.why: Most of the Pituitary Society panel prefers to continue cabergoline at the lowest effective dose (weak).

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society asks, in macroprolactinoma, for agonist response to be confirmed before conception and for surgery to be considered if there is none (strong), plus a baseline assessment (prolactin, visual fields and size) (weak). The Chinese consensus suggests shrinking a macroadenoma to microadenoma size and reports that prior treatment lowers the risk of growth in pregnancy from 18% to 4.7%.

items.stem: While a woman (fictional case) with a prolactinoma prepares for pregnancy, which contraception does the 2023 Pituitary Society suggest, and why?

options.text: Combined contraceptives, because they regularise cycles and later make it easier to date conception
options.why: The consensus advises barrier rather than hormonal methods, precisely to learn the woman’s own menstrual interval and confirm treatment efficacy.

options.text: None, because while she is not ovulating there is no risk, and the first period will show she can start trying
options.why: Pregnancy can occur before the first period; in addition, the consensus advises barrier contraception to learn the menstrual interval first.

options.text: A progestogen implant, because it does not interfere with the agonist and allows tumour response to be assessed without artefact on follow-up MRI
options.why: The consensus suggests barrier rather than hormonal methods to confirm efficacy and learn the menstrual interval.

options.text: Barrier rather than hormonal methods, to confirm treatment efficacy and learn the menstrual interval before pregnancy (weak)
options.why: Correct: this is the consensus suggestion.

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society advises barrier rather than hormonal contraception to confirm treatment efficacy and learn the menstrual interval before pregnancy (weak).

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman (fictional case) operated on for a macroprolactinoma has normal prolactin but persistent hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, and wishes to conceive. What does the 2023 Pituitary Society recommend?

options.text: Gonadotrophins, which are needed if hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism persists with normal prolactin and a wish for pregnancy (strong)
options.why: Correct: with normal prolactin, the agonist no longer solves the problem.

options.text: Increase cabergoline to 3.5 mg weekly, because the hypogonadism shows that prolactin is still biologically excessive
options.why: With normal prolactin, the consensus indicates gonadotrophins, not a higher agonist dose.

options.text: Wait for gonadal function to recover on its own, because the consensus advises against ovulation induction after pituitary surgery for macroadenoma
options.why: The consensus does not advise against it; it recommends gonadotrophins in this situation.

options.text: Bromocriptine instead of cabergoline, because ESHRE 2022 recommends it to improve reproductive outcomes in hyperprolactinaemia
options.why: Prolactin is normal, and ESHRE 2022 considers the evidence insufficient to recommend bromocriptine in recurrent pregnancy loss.

items.explanation: If hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism persists with normal prolactin and there is a wish for pregnancy, the 2023 Pituitary Society indicates gonadotrophins (strong). If surgery is done first, patients should be told of the risk of hypopituitarism (strong).

items.stem: In recurrent pregnancy loss with hyperprolactinaemia, what position does ESHRE 2022 take on bromocriptine?

options.text: It advises against it with a strong recommendation, because the available trial showed more pregnancy losses with bromocriptine than placebo
options.why: The guideline does not advise against it or grade a recommendation; “insufficient evidence to recommend” is not the same as “advises against”.

options.text: It considers the evidence (a single small trial) insufficient to recommend it, without issuing a graded recommendation
options.why: Correct: section 14.5, no recommendation.

options.text: It strongly recommends it in every woman with recurrent pregnancy loss and hyperprolactinaemia, based on several large concordant trials
options.why: There is only a single small trial, and the guideline does not consider it sufficient to recommend it.

options.text: It conditionally recommends it only until week 12 of gestation, at 2.5 mg daily
options.why: The guideline issues no such recommendation and sets no such regimen: the only study cited used 2.5-5.0 mg/day until week 9, and the evidence is considered insufficient to recommend it.

items.explanation: The ESHRE 2022 recurrent pregnancy loss guideline considers the evidence (a single small trial) insufficient to recommend bromocriptine in hyperprolactinaemia (section 14.5, no recommendation).

items.stem: On measuring prolactin during pregnancy in a woman with a prolactinoma, where do the consensus statements disagree?

options.text: Both recommend measuring it monthly in micro- and macroadenomas and ending the pregnancy if it rises by more than 50%
options.why: Neither proposes this; the Pituitary Society recommends not using it, and the Chinese consensus considers it only in macroadenomas.

options.text: The Pituitary Society measures it every 2–3 months in macroadenomas, and the Chinese consensus advises against it at any tumour size
options.why: It reverses the two consensus positions.

options.text: The Pituitary Society recommends not using it to monitor growth (strong); the Chinese consensus, in macroadenomas, suggests measuring it every 2–3 months and reading a rise > 50% with the clinical picture (weak)
options.why: Correct: this is the real disagreement.

options.text: Neither mentions prolactin in pregnancy, and both simply recommend gadolinium MRI each trimester
options.why: Both mention it, and MRI, if growth is suspected, is without gadolinium.

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society recommends not using prolactin to monitor growth in pregnancy (strong). The 2025 Chinese consensus does not recommend it in microadenomas, but in macroadenomas suggests measuring it every 2–3 months and reading a rise > 50% as possible growth with the clinical picture (very low; weak).

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) with macroprolactinoma confirms a pregnancy and stops the agonist. What follow-up does the 2023 Pituitary Society recommend?

options.text: Monthly clinical assessment and visual fields every 3 months, with MRI without gadolinium if growth is suspected (strong)
options.why: Correct: this is the schedule for macroprolactinomas.

options.text: Clinical review every 3 months, exactly as for microprolactinoma, because the risk of growth is the same at any tumour size
options.why: Three-monthly follow-up is for microprolactinomas; macroprolactinomas are reviewed monthly.

options.text: Gadolinium MRI each trimester and monthly prolactin, acting on the value even without symptoms
options.why: MRI is without gadolinium and only if growth is suspected; the Pituitary Society does not use prolactin for monitoring.

options.text: No specific monitoring until delivery, because the agonist was stopped and there is nothing more to watch
options.why: The consensus recommends monthly clinical follow-up and visual fields in macroprolactinoma (strong).

items.explanation: The 2023 Pituitary Society recommends stopping the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed (strong; in large macroprolactinomas, continuing is also an option). Microprolactinomas are followed clinically every 3 months; macroprolactinomas monthly, with visual fields every 3 months and MRI without gadolinium if growth is suspected (strong).

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) with microprolactinoma, asymptomatic after an uneventful delivery, asks whether she can breastfeed. What do the consensus statements say?

options.text: It is contraindicated in every prolactinoma, because lactation prolactin makes the tumour grow in most women
options.why: Neither contraindicates it; growth during 12 months of breastfeeding was 1.2% in microadenomas.

options.text: She can breastfeed only if she restarts cabergoline first, because both consensus statements recommend breastfeeding on the agonist to protect against tumour growth
options.why: The Chinese consensus does not recommend breastfeeding while on the agonist; if the agonist is needed, it advises stopping breastfeeding.

options.text: She can breastfeed, but with monthly prolactin and stopping breastfeeding if it exceeds 200 ng/ml
options.why: Neither proposes this monitoring; the key is whether the tumour forces the agonist to be restarted, not lactation prolactin.

options.text: She can breastfeed: it is usually not contraindicated (Pituitary Society, strong) and the Chinese consensus encourages it, although if an agonist is needed it advises stopping breastfeeding
options.why: Correct: it summarises both positions.

items.explanation: For the 2023 Pituitary Society, breastfeeding is usually not contraindicated and may be allowed for a period, depending on whether treatment must be restarted to control the mass (strong). The 2025 Chinese consensus encourages breastfeeding and, if an agonist is needed, advises stopping breastfeeding (very low; weak).

items.stem: According to the data cited by the 2025 Chinese consensus, what proportion of women with prolactinoma do not need to restart the agonist during breastfeeding?

options.text: About 10–15% of microadenomas and 30–40% of macroadenomas, so most women need to restart the agonist while breastfeeding
options.why: It inverts the proportions: the consensus gives 85–90% and 60–70% for those who do not need to restart it.

options.text: 85–90% of microadenomas and 60–70% of macroadenomas, with tumour growth over 12 months of breastfeeding of 1.2% and 4.3%
options.why: Correct: these are the consensus figures.

options.text: All women, because breastfeeding always induces prolactinoma remission and allows the agonist to be stopped permanently afterwards
options.why: It is not universal: some micro- and macroadenomas do need the agonist restarted.

options.text: 55% of microadenomas and 43% of macroadenomas, the same proportion as after agonist withdrawal in the best subgroup
options.why: 55% and 43% are Pituitary Society remission figures after withdrawal in the favourable subgroup, not lactation figures.

items.explanation: The 2025 Chinese consensus cites tumour growth over 12 months of breastfeeding of 1.2% in microadenomas and 4.3% in macroadenomas, and that 85–90% of micro- and 60–70% of macroadenomas need no agonist restart; it does not recommend breastfeeding while on the agonist. The Pituitary Society adds that after a pregnancy, treatment withdrawal may be tried (weak).

aemps-2022-dostinex-ft.title: Ficha técnica de Dostinex 0,5 mg comprimidos (cabergolina)
aemps-2022-dostinex-ft.finding: Hyperprolactinaemia: start 0.5 mg/week in 1–2 doses, increase by 0.5 mg/week at monthly intervals; usual dose 1 mg/week (0.25–2 mg); up to 4.5 mg/week has been used. Sogilen 1 and 2 mg is indicated only for Parkinson’s disease. Quinagolide (Norprolac) authorisation was revoked on 26 February 2024 and Parlodel (bromocriptine) is still marketed.
aemps-2022-dostinex-ft.limitations: Sections 4.1 and 4.2 (SmPC dated 18 February 2022). Norprolac, Parlodel and Sogilen status come from CIMA REST searches.

asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.title: Fertility evaluation of infertile women: a committee opinion
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.population: Women evaluated for infertility (including single women, same-sex couples, transgender men and non-binary patients seeking treatment); Fertil Steril 2021;116:1255–65.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.finding: Evaluation at 12 months if <35 and at 6 months if ≥35; more immediate if >40; without delay with a known condition causing infertility. Evaluate both partners at the same time, with at least one semen analysis at onset. Basic work-up: ovulation, structure and patency of the reproductive tract, and semen analysis. With regular 21–35-day cycles, ovulation confirmation is not required (unless hirsutism). Female age is the single most important predictor of fecundity. Laparoscopy, postcoital test, thrombophilia, immunological tests, karyotype, endometrial biopsy, advanced sperm function testing and prolactin are not routine. Menstrual history may suffice to establish an ovulatory pattern; oligo/amenorrhoea establishes anovulation without further ovulation testing. If history is indeterminate: luteal progesterone (≈1 week before expected menses, not a fixed day such as day 21; >3 ng/mL = presumptive evidence of recent ovulation; a single value confirms ovulation, not luteal quality), urinary LH kits (false positives in PCOS) or transvaginal ultrasound. Basal body temperature and endometrial biopsy are not routinely recommended. Prolactin not routine; indicated with galactorrhoea or oligo/amenorrhoea.
asrm-2021-fertility-evaluation.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion, not a GRADE guideline; US context; no formal strength or certainty grading.

cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.title: Chinese consensus on the diagnosis and treatment of prolactinomas (2025 edition)
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.authors: Lin S, Chen Z, Ji L, Wang L, Zhang W, Tang X, Wu Y, Fan Q, Li J, Pan L, Yao Z, Deng C, Ye H, Li S, Zhu H, Zhao Y, Wang Y, Wu ZB; China Pituitary Adenoma Specialist Council
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.population: Patients with prolactinoma (diagnosis, medical, surgical and radiation treatment, pregnancy and lactation). Panel of 60 experts from neurosurgery, endocrinology, obstetrics and gynaecology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology and methodology, supported by the MAGIC China Center (GRADE).
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.finding: Measure prolactin with menstrual disorders, infertility or galactorrhoea in women of reproductive age (low certainty; strong); sample at rest, fasting and after at least 2 h awake; repeat if < 100 ng/ml. Macroprolactin when clinical findings are discordant (low; weak); dilution to exclude the hook effect in macroadenomas (low; weak). MRI after excluding other causes (low; weak). Asymptomatic microadenoma: observe (very low; weak). Periodic echocardiography with long-term high-dose cabergoline (low; weak). Withdrawal after > 2 years on a low maintenance dose with normal prolactin and tumour shrinkage (very low; weak). Microadenoma: no need to stop the agonist while trying to conceive, but stop it once pregnancy is confirmed (very low; weak). Breastfeeding: encouraged; if the agonist is needed, stop breastfeeding (very low; weak).
cpasc-2026-prolactinoma-consensus.limitations: Full text read (Chin Neurosurg J 2026;12:17, Europe PMC version, no page numbers). Chinese national consensus led by neurosurgery; most recommendations are weak with low or very low certainty. Cabergoline is unavailable in mainland China, so bromocriptine is its first choice, which shapes several recommendations. The supplementary tables could not be read.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment. Sperm DNA fragmentation in couples with RPL: could be considered for diagnostic purposes, using a validated test (conditional; ⊕⊕⊕○). Parental karyotyping: not routine; can be carried out after an individual risk assessment (conditional).
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based. Recommendations on sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping checked in the HRO summary (hoad002) and in the justification of the full PDF. The guideline is the 2022 update (final version January 2023; HRO summary 2023); the module cites it as ESHRE 2022.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.title: Diagnosis and management of prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas: a Pituitary Society international Consensus Statement
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.authors: Petersenn S, Fleseriu M, Casanueva FF, Giustina A, Biermasz N, Biller BMK, Bronstein M, Chanson P, Fukuoka H, Gadelha M, Greenman Y, Gurnell M, Ho KKY, Honegger J, Ioachimescu AG, Kaiser UB, Karavitaki N, Katznelson L, Lodish M, Maiter D, Marcus HJ, McCormack A, Molitch M, Muir CA, Neggers S, Pereira AM, Pivonello R, Post K, Raverot G, Salvatori R, Samson SL, Shimon I, Spencer-Segal J, Vila G, Wass J, Melmed S
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.population: People with hyperprolactinaemia or prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (adults, pregnancy and fertility, children and adolescents, psychiatric disorders, menopause). International multidisciplinary Pituitary Society workshop with experts from 13 countries.
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.finding: Investigate prolactin with infertility, new menstrual irregularity, amenorrhoea or galactorrhoea (strong). With prolactin < 5 times the upper limit, repeat the measurement; use cannulated sampling if stress is suspected (strong). Review drugs, hypothyroidism, renal or liver failure and pregnancy (strong). Test macroprolactin when the rise is moderate (< 200 ng/ml), at least when clinical or imaging findings are discordant (strong); 1:100 dilution for a giant adenoma with normal or mildly raised prolactin (strong). MRI once hyperprolactinaemia is confirmed if no other cause is evident (strong). Cabergoline is the preferred agonist (strong). Echocardiography by dose (> 2.0 mg/week: baseline and every 2–3 years; ≤ 2.0 mg/week: after 5–6 years) (weak). Consider withdrawal with low doses, > 2 years of treatment and adenoma shrinkage (strong). Stop the agonist once pregnancy is confirmed (strong); do not use prolactin to monitor growth in pregnancy (strong); breastfeeding is usually not contraindicated (strong).
petersenn-2023-prolactinoma-consensus.limitations: Full PDF read (Nat Rev Endocrinol 2023;19:722-740). Expert consensus by vote; grades “strong” (moderate or high evidence) and “weak” (low or very low) per Box 1 (p. 724), with no per-recommendation GRADE certainty. Literature up to January 2023. The supplementary boxes (including the pregnancy and withdrawal discussion) could not be read. Pituitary Society statement; not a fertility guideline.
